The words

In these our days so perilous,
Lord, peace in mercy send us;
No God but Thee can fight for us,
No God but Thee defend us;
Thou our only God and Savior.

How to sing it from the solfa

  • Find doh first. Play or hum F and sing d r m f s up from it, so the whole choir has the key in their ears before you start.
  • Pitch the first note. The tune starts on r (G).
  • Count the time. 4/4 means four crotchet beats in each bar. In the grid every cell is half a crotchet: a dash (–) holds the note before it, and _ is a rest.
  • Know the notes. The tune uses d r m f s l and the chromatic de. A comma after a note (s,) is the octave below; an apostrophe (d') is the octave above.

About the hymn

The words are by Martin Luther, first published in 600. The English translation is by Richard Massie (1854). The tune, VERLEIH UNS FRIEDEN GNÄDIGLICH, is by Martin Luther (1533). This version of the melody and the words comes from the Open Hymnal Project.

  • Words (600): Traditional Latin
  • Words (600): Martin Luther (1483–1546)
  • Translated (1854): Richard Massie (1800–1887)
  • Music (1533): Martin Luther (1483–1546)

Questions about In These Our Days So Perilous

What is the doh of In These Our Days So Perilous?

In this version, in F major, doh is F. If your choir sings it in another key, doh moves to the new key note and every solfa syllable stays the same — that is what movable doh means.

What note does In These Our Days So Perilous start on?

It starts on r (G in F major). Find doh first, then sing up or down to r.

Is In These Our Days So Perilous in the public domain?

Yes. Martin Luther died in 1546, Richard Massie died in 1887, Martin Luther died in 1546; the words were first published in 1854 and the music in 1533. Everyone named died before 1955 and both were published before 1929, so the hymn is out of copyright in Nigeria, the UK, the EU and the United States. Modern arrangements and translations can still be under copyright.
